planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; raised beds help offset Elsanta's susceptibility to crown rot in wet ground.

directions: Elsanta was bred in the Netherlands and released in the early 1980s, quickly becoming the dominant commercial and garden strawberry across the UK, Netherlands, Belgium, and much of Western Europe, a position it still holds in many regions decades later. It produces large, glossy, conical, bright red berries with a classic sweet-tart flavor when allowed to ripen fully on the plant, though fruit picked underripe can taste comparatively bland. Plants are vigorous and heavy-yielding but relatively susceptible to crown rot and red core (Phytophthora) in poorly drained soil, so raised beds and good drainage are important for a healthy planting. Renovate beds after harvest by removing old foliage and excess runners to keep plantings productive for several seasons.
sources: NIAB (National Institute of Agricultural Botany, UK)

common_name: Cambridge Favourite Strawberry (Classic English Garden Standard)

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Cambridge Favourite tolerates a wide range of garden soils better than most heirloom cultivars.

directions: Cambridge Favourite was released in the 1950s from a strawberry breeding program in Cambridge, England, and went on to become one of the most widely grown garden strawberries in the United Kingdom for the remainder of the twentieth century. It is valued less for exceptional flavor than for its dependable, heavy mid-season cropping, reasonable tolerance of mildew, and adaptability to a wide range of garden soils and situations. The medium-sized, bright orange-red berries are firm enough to hold up well to freezing and preserving as well as fresh eating. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing off old foliage and thinning runners to keep plantings vigorous for several years.
sources: NIAB (National Institute of Agricultural Botany, UK)

common_name: Oso Grande Strawberry (Extra-Large California Short-Day Classic)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Oso Grande is a University of California-bred short-day cultivar long grown across the mild-winter South and California for its very large, firm fruit.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Oso Grande was released in the late 1980s by the University of California strawberry breeding program and became one of the standard short-day, extra-large-fruited cultivars grown across the mild-winter South and California for decades. Its very large, firm, glossy conical berries hold their size and shape well through a long picking season, and the sturdy fruit ships and stores better than many older, softer-fruited cultivars. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual, setting out fresh crowns in October or November for a harvest that runs from late winter into spring. Maintain consistent drip irrigation and raised, well-drained beds to limit the disease pressure common in humid Gulf Coast strawberry plantings.
sources: University of California, Davis strawberry breeding program

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Pajaro is a 1979 University of California release that was once among the most widely planted short-day strawberries in the state.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Pajaro was released in 1979 by the University of California strawberry breeding program and was, for much of the 1980s and 1990s, one of the most widely planted short-day strawberries in California, valued for its glossy, dark red, firm conical berries and good flavor. Though newer patented cultivars have largely replaced it in commercial production, Pajaro remains available to home gardeners and small growers in mild-winter regions who appreciate its dependable vigor and old-fashioned strawberry flavor. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual, setting out fresh crowns in October or November for a harvest running from late winter into spring.
sources: University of California, Davis strawberry breeding program

common_name: Gaviota Strawberry (Early, Sweet California Short-Day Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns in October–November in zone 9 for a winter-into-spring crop; Gaviota is a University of California-bred short-day cultivar prized among home gardeners for exceptionally sweet flavor rather than shipping toughness.

directions: Plant dormant crowns with the crown at soil level in raised, well-drained beds in full sun; Gaviota is a short-day strawberry from the University of California breeding program, prized among home gardeners and farmers-market growers for exceptionally sweet, aromatic flavor that many tasters rank above more widely shipped commercial cultivars. Its dark red, glossy berries ripen earlier in the season than many other short-day types but are softer and less shelf-stable, making it better suited to home use and local sales than long-distance shipping. Because it is a short-day type, Gulf Coast gardeners get the best results treating it as a fall-planted winter annual. Pick promptly since the soft ripe fruit is more prone to rot in humid conditions than firmer cultivars.
sources: University of California, Davis strawberry breeding program

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; a winter straw mulch protects crowns in the coldest parts of its range.

directions: Governor Simcoe was bred at the Vineland research station in Ontario, Canada, and became a widely grown June-bearing cultivar across Canadian and northern U.S. home gardens for decades after its release, valued for large, firm, richly flavored berries on vigorous, winter-hardy plants. It produces a concentrated mid-season harvest and holds up well both for fresh eating and preserving, a combination that kept it in wide cultivation long after many contemporaries from the same era fell out of favor. Its cold hardiness suits it to prairie and northern climates where many modern patented cultivars struggle to overwinter reliably. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to sustain productivity in following years.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs
